We're getting ready to launch the first phase of the website and I thought I would get some ideas here. League for Gamers aims to help bring positivity back to gaming and represent the consumer for advocacy with publishers and lawmakers.

The first step is to be a robust club or hangout for video game players. We have 1500 signed up so far, and will be opening profile pages and LFG updates on the site this month. Next wave we will add follows and message posting by all users. It will work like a mini social network for gamers.

By being a member, you will be able to participate in various activities or projects that LFG will co-ordinate in the future. Projects might include:

  • Fundraising for gaming related charities
  • E-mail or call-in campaigns to lawmakers on legislation that affects games/internet
  • voting on games (we hope to host a gamers' choice award for indie and AAA games)
  • Volunteer projects to expand LFG itself
  • Bringing new devs together into small indie teams, providing educational resources
  • Co-ordinating the fundraising and establishment of gaming research to show the positive effects of gaming.

The idea is that there might be several projects through the year, each run by small groups of volunteers that belong to the main membership.

What projects would you like to see?
What would you like to see League For Gamers tackle first?
One person suggested that we link your Steam profile to our profile pages. Can do! Just not an immediate goal for us, but we're going to look at it after messaging goes in.

I would like to see a PR department come into full swing, giving networks and others easy 'lazy' counter voices to the SJW crowd, who make themselves so readily available and easy to interview, to fight against the anti-gamer narrative. We need fresh, composed faces who can get in front of cameras easily.

LFG is going to be neutral in the GG debate, even if I am not. The advocacy we will be doing will mostly be consumer representation, not really countering SJWs. Still there are things that LFG can do that are related. One is research...having more data to use.

The other is a little project we have going right now: Encouraged by E3 discussions on female protagonists, we are doing an info poster. The poster will show 25 years of female positive gaming, showing the games with female protagonists and possibly the ratio as well. The infographic will be free online and we'll sell a poster version to help defray costs. This is already in progress.

So, we can approach these issues in a different way than how GG does it.

I'm not talking in terms of a GG thing, but rather, a counter voice to people saying 'games cause misogyny and sexism', which gets perpetuated because the people who do so are professional glory hounds who will plop themselves in front of a camera and give people a story whenever they want. If someone attacks comics, figures like Neil Gaiman or representatives of the Comic Book Legal Defense Fund are there to be the other talking head.
Yes, I'd like to find some well spoken and aggressive advocates who can speak on behalf of LFG. Suggestions?

You could begin by just compiling existing media personalities with a track record into a list, with their consent, as a 'counterpoint' list with contact information to give to media outlets or provide to them should they fail in a report to provide both sides.

  • Milo, obviously
  • Liz F
  • Oliver Campbell (I'm sure he could use the appearance fees)
  • Brandon Morse

That's really the idea. LFG is being designed to let sub-groups or cells to run these various projects on their own.

As far as I am concerned, this is a good way forward. Empowers the users, makes the league all the more relevant, and adds to its relative power by giving it away partially. I'd like to see the group advocate for two things:

First and foremost is Consumer Rights. Steam giving refunds is a nice first step, but the big three consoles are still sorely lacking in the "This game is broke, I want a refund" department. League for Gamers should be about giving the consumer more rights.

There needs to be a well reasoned and intelligent response to the creator shamers i.e. McIntosh, Sarkeesian, and people who would profit off of not just being offended by art but lying about it in the process (FemFreq's Hitman video is pretty much nothing but a lie).
